children.topic:
1. Splenomegaly
Etiology & Classifications

Key Fact: Largest lymphatic organ.
Not palpable unless enlarged 2-3x its normal size
A. Causes of Huge Spleen

Bilharziasis (Schistosomiasis):
Portal hypertension drives splenic congestion
+ RES hyperplasia from bilharzial toxins

Hematologic Malignancy:
Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)
and Myelofibrosis

Infections:
Kala-Azar (Leishmaniasis)
and Chronic Malaria

Congenital Hemolytic:
Thalassemia Major

Circulatory/Metabolic:
Polycythemia Rubra Vera
and Gaucher Disease

B. Causes of Tender Spleen
(TIBS Mnemonic)
T — Typhoid fever
I — Infective endocarditis
B — Brucellosis
S — Septicemia
C. General Etiological Categories

Infectious:
Bacterial (T.B., Syphilis),
Viral (Infectious Mononucleosis),
Parasitic (Hydatid cyst),
Protozoal (Malaria, Kala-Azar)

Circulatory:
Portal hypertension causing
congestive splenomegaly

Metabolic:
Gaucher disease, Amyloidosis,
Rickets, Porphyria

Tumors:
Benign (Hemangioma, Lymphangioma)
Malignant (Lymphoma, Fibrosarcoma)

Collagen Vascular:
Felty Syndrome

2. Hypersplenism
(Splenic Hyperfunction)

Definition: Pathological hyperfunction
with premature sequestration and destruction
of blood cells, resulting in pancytopenia
(anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia)
Etiology

Primary:
Idiopathic (no identifiable cause)

Secondary:
Portal hypertension (congestive)
or autoimmune (Felty syndrome)
Diagnostic Workup

Peripheral Blood Smear:
Confirms pancytopenia

Bone Marrow Aspiration:
Shows compensatory hypercellularity
(increased megakaryocytes
and erythroid precursors)

Radioactive Isotopic Studies:
Chromium-51 tagging of RBCs shows
diminished erythrocyte half-life and
concentrated radioactivity over spleen
(proves spleen is primary clearance site)
Management

Primary Hypersplenism:
Splenectomy is curative

Secondary Hypersplenism:
Treat the underlying cause.
Splenectomy rarely first-line
unless medically refractory

3. Splenectomy
Indications
Category I: Definite (Absolute)

1. Severe/shattered splenic trauma
(hemodynamic instability, non-salvageable)

2. Splenic abscess
(unresponsive to antibiotics/drainage)

3. Hydatid cyst
(high rupture and anaphylaxis risk)

4. Splenic venous thrombosis
(causes left-sided portal HTN
and isolated gastric varices.
Splenectomy is curative)

5. Splenic artery aneurysm
(high rupture risk)

6. En bloc resection
(oncological margin for adjacent cancers:
stomach or pancreatic tail neoplasms)
7. Primary splenic neoplasm
Category II: Desirable

8. Hereditary Spherocytosis
(gold-standard definitive cure,
prevents hemolytic crises
and pigment gallstones)

9. ITP
(if persisted >6-9 months and
failed corticosteroid therapy)

10. Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
(upon failure, contraindication, or
severe complications of steroids)

11. Gastro-esophageal Devascularization
(Hassab-Kairy procedure for
bleeding esophageal varices)
Category III: Debatable

12. Small splenic cysts
(often conservative unless symptomatic)

13. Thalassemia Major
(to decrease splenic sequestration
and lower transfusion requirements)

14. Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic
Purpura (TTP)

4. Critical Surgical
Precautions

A. Platelet Transfusion Rule
(Thrombocytopenic States)

Rule: Platelet transfusions must ONLY
be given AFTER the safety ligature
of the splenic artery is tied and secure

Reason: If transfused before ligation,
the hyperactive spleen immediately
sequesters and destroys the platelets,
rendering transfusion useless and
increasing microvascular clotting risk

B. Search for Accessory
Spleens (Splenules)

Must: Meticulously scan abdomen
during splenectomy for hemolytic
or thrombocytopenic disorders

Common Locations:
Splenic hilum (50%),
Splenic vessels/tail of pancreas (30%),
Splenic ligaments or mesocolon

If Missed: Accessory spleen undergoes
rapid compensatory hypertrophy
causing complete clinical recurrence
of the primary hematological disease
C. Operating Room Prep

At least 2 units of matched blood
must be physically present in the OR
before making an incision (elective cases)

5. Post-Splenectomy
Complications

1. Reactionary Hemorrhage:
Severe bleeding in immediate
postoperative hours due to a
slipped ligature of the splenic pedicle

2. Subphrenic Abscess/Collection:
Caused by poor surgical hemostasis
or fluid accumulation in the
left subdiaphragmatic space

3. Left Basal Lung Collapse
& Atelectasis:
Diaphragmatic splinting
and left-sided pain

4. Gastric Fistula:
Ischemic necrosis of gastric wall
from damage to short gastric vessels
during ligation along gastrosplenic ligament

5. Pancreatic Fistula & Abscess:
Pancreatic tail extends into lienorenal
ligament and splenic hilum.
If tail is accidentally crushed, ligated,
or divided, pancreatic enzymes leak
causing subphrenic abscess and fistula

6. Hematologic Alterations:
Marked leukocytosis and thrombocytosis
(reactive rise due to loss of
splenic destruction reservoir)

7. Portal Vein Thrombosis:
Clot propagates retrogradely from
the ligated splenic vein stump

6. Overwhelming
Post-Splenectomy Infection
(OPSI / OPSS)

Pathophysiology:
Spleen removal eliminates the primary site
of IgM production and non-specific opsonins
(Tuftsin and Properdin). Without these,
the immune system cannot clear
encapsulated organisms, leading to
rapid bacteremia and septic shock
Risk: 2% lifetime mortality risk
Primary Pathogens

1. Streptococcus pneumoniae
(most common and lethal)
2. Neisseria meningitidis
3. Haemophilus influenzae
OPSI Prophylaxis Guidelines

Vaccinations:
Polyvalent pneumococcal,
meningococcal, and
H. influenzae type B vaccines (mandatory)
Timing:

Elective Surgery:
Vaccinate 2 weeks prior to surgery

Emergency Trauma Surgery:
Vaccinate exactly 2 weeks post-operatively
(to allow immune recovery and
maximize antibody titers)
or prior to hospital discharge

Antibiotic Prophylaxis:
Daily oral penicillin or amoxicillin
for at least 2 years post-splenectomy
in pediatric patients under age 15
